newsitem.title: JAPAN: Rubber - Stock falls, Thai offer to help Japan prices.
newsitem.headline: Rubber - Stock falls, Thai offer to help Japan prices.

text.p: Japanese rubber futures markets will be supported this week by a stronger offer price from Thailand and falling stocks in Japan, traders said on Monday.
But the price gains are likely to be limited, and trading is becoming quieter ahead of the seasonal holidays, they said.
The benchmark May contract on the Tokyo Commodity Exchange (TOCOM) ended Monday's morning session at 146.3 yen per kg, against 146.0 yen at Friday's close.
The Kobe Rubber Exchange's May contract was at 146.4 yen per kg, compared with 145.8 yen on Friday.
"We were encouraged by the stronger offer price for Thai rubber, and some investors generated buying orders," a rubber trader in Tokyo said.
The offer price for Thai rubber to Japan was quoted at about $1.25 to $1.26 per kg on a free-on-board basis on Monday, up from $1.22 a week earlier.
Rainfall in Thailand late last week, which has started to disrupt the rubber tapping process, was the main reason for the stronger offer price, traders said.
Falls in Japan's rubber stocks are also a bullish factor, but further drops are seen needed to prop up the market.

Japan's rubber stocks at designated warehouses steadily increased to this year's high of 47,873 tonnes at the end of September from 25,976 tonnes in early January, Rubber Trade Association of Japan data shows.
The stocks at the end of November totalled 39,698 tonnes, the first time they had fallen below 40,000 since mid-August.

"Buyers certainly welcomed the recent falls of domestic stocks. But we need further drops of 4,000 to 5,000 tonnes in order to support the market," a brokerage house analyst said. "We don't expect drastic price rallies in the near term."
Nearby months on the Japanese rubber futures markets will remain volatile this week, ahead of the spot month's expiry on December 20, traders said.
"Local investors will continue to liquidate positions throughout this week, influencing other contracts," another brokerage house analyst said.
Open interest of the Tokyo rubber market totalled 196,386 lots as of December 12, the first time they had fallen below 200,000 lots since August 15, 1994. Of that, spot December had 10,134 lots.
